name: Dana Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and still a junior agent on the contact-centre phone and chat queue. I finished secondary school and started here after years working in a hotel breakfast room. I am quick to try a new screen and use the approved AI sorter every day, but I still ask a colleague to check me when a customer has changed a booking twice. My pay is low for the job, and I know I am learning more slowly on the difficult cases than the experienced agents.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life like after you leave the queue?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Pavel does casual grounds work, and our grown children have their own households. We rent a flat and have three weeks of expenses saved. Few other call-centre jobs are nearby. I hope to stop working long hours eventually, but I have no wage replacement settled; the call I remember is the one where a customer paid twice and my tidy first answer missed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the afternoon queue AI Plateau looks much like the sorter I use every day. I would still check the actual payment line when it gives me a smooth answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can keep learning here, but our three-week reserve makes every quiet grounds-work week a worry. A tool saving minutes does not pay the flat rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking routine booking chats and checking the AI sorter against payment records. In the first year of small change, Pavel and I would cancel the extra television package and put that amount into a rent account each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the job, worried about money. A fast reply can still leave a second charge on the customer’s card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which payment did the sorter miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Monday the sorter pulled the first payment but missed another one made a minute later. I asked a senior agent to check the ledger before I promised a refund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cut that package?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pavel (my partner) and I watch ordinary television enough. We can cut the extra package without asking our grown children for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues Steady Disruption will remove easy booking chats before it removes the need to correct wrong ones. I would join a joint request for paid correction hours and a way customers can reach a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior hours could be cut before I get good at the complex calls. Pavel’s grounds jobs change with the weather, so a short paid rota would put rent in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d learn the new booking checker by running fifteen old changed bookings through it on a paid shift if the supervisor lets us log wrong answers. I’d also sign the staff group’s demand for paid correction time; in the first year easy chats move, I’d apply for posted paid reception work only if written weekly wage and hours cover rent and bills, keeping paid calls until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I want to test the new checker myself. If the easy chats go, I lose the work that lets a junior agent practise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group show management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count wrong dates and the calls that come back after a machine reply. A technical error list alone will not protect the paid hours, so the staff group must ask for them together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge reception pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the posted full week, not just the hourly rate. If I am offered two good-looking shifts, our rent is still due for seven days.

I know our **three-week reserve** cannot carry a long rent gap.
do: Test **fifteen changed bookings** with the new checker on paid time only if supervisor permits error logging.
Sign the **staff group demand** for paid correction time and human access in 2026.

steps.text: Test fifteen changed bookings with new checker on paid time if supervisor permits error logging

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2028 could answer nearly all the simple booking chats I am paid to do. I would ask for posted paid openings and the date our rota changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior place could disappear in 2028, however quickly I learn a screen. Robots around 2031 are a later risk for physical work, and three weeks saved cannot carry a rent gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d delay replacing our usable hallway cupboard and keep that money with our three-week savings. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid clinic-laundry job only if written weekly wage and hours cover rent and travel; I’d take a paid trial if offered and leave calls only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but I could still look at a real laundry shift. Three weeks in the bank is not enough time to learn whether a rumoured job is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a laundry trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would try a full paid shift loading, sorting and recording clean sheets. Robots could reach that hands-on work around 2031, so I would not tell Pavel it is a lifetime shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the cupboard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pavel (my partner) and I can mend the cupboard door. We would leave the replacement money with our savings for rent.

I’d say **2028 AGI** could take simple booking chats.
think: I think my **junior place** could disappear in 2028.
I know **three weeks saved** cannot cover a long rent gap.
do: Delay the **usable cupboard** replacement in 2026 and keep its money with our three-week savings.
Seek **posted paid clinic laundry** after 2028 only with written wage and hours covering rent and travel.
Take a **paid trial** if offered and leave calls only after a suitable signed offer.
feel: **Alarmed**, able to inspect a paid trial if offered.
S2.quote: Three weeks in the bank is not enough time to learn whether a rumoured job is real.
fieldNote: She sees **2031 robots** as a later laundry risk.

A **paid full shift** would reveal loading and sorting demands.

steps.text: Delay usable hallway cupboard replacement and retain its money for rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2031 gives us time to win real paid learning hours for jobs outside the phone queue. I would ask the staff group to demand posted roles and paid course time together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn clinic laundry work before 2031, though robots around 2034 could later reach the loading. I can try new tools early, but I will not pay for a course while our rent depends on both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d join the group demand and take an employer-funded laundry-safety course on paid time only if a posted paid clinic vacancy requires it. In the first year after 2031, I’d accept that job only on a signed offer with written weekly wage and hours covering rent and travel; otherwise I’d keep paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with time to inspect a real opening. A course certificate without a paid laundry shift will not buy our groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the safety course need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to sort a load with the trainer and learn how to mark contaminated items without guessing. If the lesson is only a slideshow, I would ask to practise before taking a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Pavel check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Pavel (my partner) the posted wage and paid class hours before enrolling. His grounds work has no fixed rota, so we need a week we can actually cover.

I’d ask for **paid learning hours** before leaving calls.
think: I think I could learn **laundry work** before 2031.
I know **2034 robots** may later reach that physical work.
I cannot fund **unpaid study** on our current rent budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives the centre time to plan paid junior hours instead of waiting for a sudden cut. I would ask colleagues to sign the same request for yearly rosters and paid coaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I may be closer to stopping full-time work by 2036, but I do not know what income would replace our wages. Three weeks saved makes the next rent bill hard enough without promising myself a future pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking booking chats and help colleagues send a joint written request for yearly paid junior hours and coaching. In the first year after 2036, if my call hours fall, I’d move to a posted paid front-desk job only on a signed offer showing written weekly wage and hours covering rent and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later work, anxious about today’s rent. A decade before AGI reaches my queue does not turn three weeks of savings into retirement money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What coaching figure matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how many actual paid coaching shifts a new person gets. A video link is not someone to catch a wrong second charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the grown children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children manage their own bills. I would share supper with them, but I would not put their wages into our rent plan.

steps.text: Keep taking paid booking chats while shifts remain

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could answer the routine chats I rely on while I am still learning the exceptions. Three weeks saved cannot carry our rent through a long search. I would need written paid-hour notice, a posted paid vacancy with weekly wage and hours covering rent and bills, a paid trial, and funded training on paid time if that vacancy requires it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether the customer gets another person when the first AI reply is wrong. My daughter has her own rent to pay, so I cannot plan for her to cover ours.

headlineQuote: My daughter has her own rent to pay, so I cannot plan for her to cover ours.
portrait: At **58**, Dana is a junior contact-centre agent after secondary school and hotel work.
She and Pavel have **three weeks saved**, low pay and few nearby call jobs.
She uses **AI daily** but still needs help with complicated booking changes.
Her **grown children** have separate households; she does not budget for their support.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could take routine chats before she masters the exceptions.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid-hour notice**, rent-covering posted work, paid trial and funded required training would help.
